source_lines.35: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M=H_-\cup_\varphi H_+$ be a Heegaard splitting of a closed oriented smooth $3$-manifold, let $\Sigma=\partial H_-=\partial H_+$, and let $c\subset\Sigma$ be an embedded circle with a chosen annular neighbourhood. If $\varphi$ is replaced by $\varphi\circ\tau_c$ or $\varphi\circ\tau_c^{-1}$, where $\tau_c$ is a Dehn twist in the chosen annular coordinates, the resulting oriented $3$-manifold is obtained from $M$ by one surgery on a knot $K$ obtained by pushing $c$ into the interior of $H_-$. The annulus between $c$ and the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood of $K$ supplies a framing; the surgery meridian is identified with $\mu+ \lambda_A$ or $\mu-\lambda_A$, according to the twist direction, where $\mu$ is the meridian of $K$ and $\lambda_A$ is the parallel determined by that annulus. Thus the surgery coefficient relative to this framing is integral with absolute value $1$.

source_lines.88: 1.2 Let $M=E_K(p/q)$ and choose a bicollar of the gluing torus. Thickening the exterior and attached solid torus across this collar gives an open cover of $M$ whose two sets retract to the pieces and whose intersection retracts to $T_K$. Write $\alpha=p\mu+q\lambda$, and choose $\beta=r\mu+s\lambda$ with $ps-qr=1$, so $\alpha,\beta$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. In the Mayer–Vietoris map, $\alpha$ maps to $(p[\mu],0)$ because it bounds the attached solid-torus meridian disk, and $\beta$ maps to $(r[\mu],\pm v)$ where $v$ generates the first homology of the attached solid torus; the coefficient is $\pm1$ because $\beta$ intersects $\alpha$ once. The pieces and their overlap are path-connected: the exterior is a connected manifold and hence path-connected, and the solid torus and boundary torus are path-connected. By [F6], the following $H_0$ map sends $1$ to $(1,-1)$ and is injective. Exactness therefore identifies $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ with the cokernel of the $H_1$ map. source_lines.84: 3.2 If $c$ separates $F$, cutting gives a component $F_K$ containing the knot boundary and a component $F_0$ with boundary $c$. Let their genera be $h_K,h_0$. Since $F_K$ has two boundary components and $F_0$ has one, Euler characteristic additivity along the cut and [F2] give $g(F)=h_K+h_0$. Cap $F_K$ by a parallel copy of $D$ and discard $F_0$. If $h_0>0$ this is a lower genus spanning surface, contradiction; if $h_0=0$, it is another minimum genus surface with fewer intersection circles, contradicting the choice in step 1.2. The cap is embedded after rounding in the local product neighbourhood from step 2.1. Thus no circle can occur. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.86: 4.1 With no circles, $F\cap S=\alpha$. Since $S$ separates the two knot pieces in the standard sum model, the proper arc $\alpha$ separates $F$ into two connected surfaces $F_1,F_2$, each with one boundary component. Cutting along an arc increases total Euler characteristic by $1$, so [F2] gives $g(F)=g(F_1)+g(F_2)$. The two surfaces are connected because any component of either side not incident to $\alpha$ would already be a separate component of $F$; the sole arc has just one collar on each side. Their boundary circles consist of the corresponding knot subarc and $\alpha\subset S$, and hence represent $K$ and $J$ by [L1] and the original connected-sum datum. Thus $g(K)+g(J)\le g(F_1)+g(F_2)=g(F)=g(K\#J)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the full equality. [given, F2, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
